title: AI investment is already large while broad productivity gains remain difficult to detect
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Federal Reserve staff researchers find a striking difference between the strength of AI infrastructure spending and the evidence that generative AI has already changed economy-wide productivity or employment. Data centres, computer equipment and power are attracting capital, and some input prices have risen sharply. Use of AI is spreading, but relatively few employees use it every day. The authors judge that much of the recent acceleration in U.S. productivity predates the diffusion of generative AI. Their November assessment leaves room for large later effects without assuming that present investment, prospective economic benefits and eventual profits for model developers are interchangeable.

Announced U.S. data-centre plans amounted to nearly $300 billion in 2024 and more than $1 trillion in 2025. The amounts are proposed project costs, including equipment. Figure 2 converts announcements available through May 2026 into spending paths using historical cancellation rates and construction schedules. If new plans continue at a pace similar to the recent one, annualized investment rises from about $100 billion in 2024 to over $880 billion by the end of 2027, exceeding 2% of GDP. Alternative paths assume new plans arrive at twice or a quarter of the recent pace. About one-third of investment goes to structures, with most of the rest going to equipment. Imports offset part of the contribution to domestic output. The authors put the import share at around half. Grid connection queues, zoning, turbine and chip availability and construction labour can delay or prevent completion (section 3, figures 1–3).

Financing is changing alongside the volume. Large cloud providers initially used cash flow but increasingly issued debt and used financing backed by long-term leases. The paper sees little evidence thus far that non-AI investment has fallen below its longer-term growth pace. Nor does it assign a broad rise in long-term yields to this borrowing alone. Concentrated demand has already affected prices in exposed categories, including memory and storage. Wholesale electricity costs may rise in some markets. The size and timing of any effect on consumer power prices are harder to establish (sections 3 and 5).

The authors estimate that three frontier labs had at least $107 billion in annualized revenue in the third quarter, equivalent to around 19% of software-sector gross output. Their lower bound relies on unaudited disclosures and estimates, including partial coverage of one lab. Annualizing a recent month is different from recording a year of sales. Two companies reported gross margins on inference of approximately 30–40%. What remains after serving users must fund research, training and overhead, including larger successor models. Faster demand and cheaper computation can help, but a profitable model need not make the developer cash-generative while development spending rises (section 4).

Over 40% of workers in several surveys reported using AI at work, yet only around 10% used it daily. Firm surveys returned estimates from about 20% to 78%, reflecting different question wording, firm sizes and weighting. Exposure of an occupation’s tasks also says little by itself about whether a worker is replaced, retrained or becomes more productive. Some studies find weaker hiring or employment for junior workers in exposed occupations. Firm surveys and other studies find little aggregate employment effect. Task-level efficiency gains are clearer, especially for less experienced workers who remain employed. Translating gains on individual tasks into finished output requires complementary changes in workflows and skills. The authors therefore distinguish a plausible future boost to productive capacity from measurable aggregate gains to date (sections 4 and 6–8).

questions.question: How much planned data-centre spending will produce operating capacity on schedule?
questions.detail: The central spending path relies on past cancellation and construction experience. New sites may have different power and equipment constraints. Match project announcements to construction permits, utility interconnection agreements, equipment orders and company capital-expenditure disclosures. Distinguish contracted capacity from energized sites and domestic value added from imports. Those comparisons would narrow the timing and size of demand for infrastructure suppliers.

questions.question: When can inference revenues cover successive rounds of model development?
questions.detail: The paper’s lower-bound revenue run rate rests on company statements, and its gross margin estimates exclude major costs. Seek dated financial statements, debt offering documents, lease commitments and disclosures on inference usage, pricing and training expenditure. Separate recurring cash collections from capacity commitments and current-model costs from spending on replacements. That would help assess the funding requirement and the allocation of returns between infrastructure owners and model providers.

questions.question: Does intensive adoption raise final output once the slowest stages of production are included?
questions.detail: Worker surveys establish broad experimentation and task studies find efficiency improvements, but few workers use AI every day. Consult the cited Census business surveys and employer-level records of adoption, hours, output quality and completed sales. Compare organizations with similar pre-adoption growth and follow both new hires and incumbents. This would test whether better task performance supports higher sustainable margins or only faster intermediate work.
